final_answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
TO: Janet Morales, General Counsel (cc: Allison Trask, Whitfield & Crane LLP) | RE: Proposed termination of Marcus D. Washington, SVP Operations | BASIS: matter documents through the June 3, 2024 email; target separation June 10, 2024.

1. BOTTOM LINE
Do not terminate on June 10. Risk is HIGH. The termination cannot presently be defended as performance-based or as a bona fide position elimination without material exposure to (a) OSH Act s.11(c) and Illinois retaliatory-discharge/whistleblower claims, (b) ADEA/IHRA age discrimination supported by the CEO's own words, (c) workers' compensation retaliation (820 ILCS 305/4(h)), and (d) breach of contract if "Cause" is asserted. Cause is not viable. The only defensible route is termination without Cause under s.4.2 (about $375,000 plus Accrued Obligations), after an independent investigation, a properly closed or extended PIP, 30 days' written notice, and a counsel-negotiated release.

2. KEY FACTS
- 11/15/23: Kessler: "fresh energy... leaders who grew up with technology"; Ostrowski says he is "blocked at the SVP level" (predates protected activity).
- Dec 2023: Washington questions safety of Lean 2.0 changes. 1/8/24: written safety complaint (copied to Kessler). 1/22: Kessler says she will rate him "Needs Improvement": "different era... doesn't have the runway left"; HR warned it sounded age-related.
- 2/2: Safety Committee finds two of five changes raise compliance concerns. 2/5: Ostrowski to Kessler: committee "overly conservative"; Washington "blocking"; complaint is "slow-walk[ing]"; asks to proceed with all five.
- 2/15: first-ever NI in 22 years. 3/5: OSHA 11(c) complaint (HR copied 3/6). 3/18: PIP. 4/3: workers' comp claim. 5/17: PIP ends: 1 of 3 objectives fully met; 8 of 12 facilities done (four Tennessee/Georgia sites delayed by OSHA inspections); cost down 6.4% vs 12% target.
- 5/20: HR recommends 30-day extension; Kessler declines same day. 5/22: HR memorializes risks. 5/28: restructuring memo. 6/3: Kessler orders separation by 6/10 and asks to "explore... Cause" to avoid full severance.

3. OSH ACT s.11(c) (29 U.S.C. 660(c)) - HIGH
- Internal complaint, refusal to implement, and the OSHA complaint are protected. Knowledge: Kessler received the 1/8 complaint and 2/5 email; HR had the OSHA complaint 3/6. Open: whether Kessler knew before the 3/18 PIP.
- Causation is "but for," not sole cause (29 C.F.R. 1977.6(b)). Evidence: Ostrowski's email ties the complaint to "blocking"; the review penalizes the December safety objection; PIP objective 1 required rollout of the changes he protested; PIP issued 13 days after filing.
- No private action; the Secretary sues for reinstatement and back pay. A termination can be added to the pending OSHA complaint within 30 days and would likely escalate the investigation.
- Company's best fact: the 11/15/23 discussion predates the complaint, suggesting a pre-existing plan. It helps here but hurts on age (item 5). Also unknown: what triggered the southern-facility OSHA inspections.

4. ILLINOIS RETALIATORY DISCHARGE / WHISTLEBLOWER - HIGH
- Tort for discharge violating clear public policy (Palmateer v. International Harvester, 85 Ill. 2d 124 (1981); Kelsay v. Motorola, 74 Ill. 2d 172 (1978)); a valid non-pretextual reason breaks causation (Clemons v. Mechanical Devices, 184 Ill. 2d 328 (1998)). Safety reporting fits; punitive damages available; the contract's at-will clause is no defense.
- Illinois Whistleblower Act (740 ILCS 174/20) bars retaliation for refusing to participate in unlawful activity. 2025 amendments broadening internal-report protection apply only to later conduct.

5. AGE DISCRIMINATION (ADEA 29 U.S.C. 623; IHRA 775 ILCS 5/2-102) - HIGH
- Washington is 58. Decisionmaker statements: "fresh energy," "grew up with technology," "different era," "runway"; Board memo: "digitally native," "energy, adaptability, and runway," "grew up in a data-driven environment." Courts weigh evidence holistically (Ortiz v. Werner Enterprises, 834 F.3d 760 (7th Cir. 2016)); ADEA requires but-for causation (Gross v. FBL Financial, 557 U.S. 167 (2009)), which pretext can supply (Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing, 530 U.S. 133 (2000)). HR warned Kessler; she did not retract. Willful violation doubles damages.
- Replacement Ostrowski's age is not in the record; determine it.
- Counter: technology fluency is not age (Hazen Paper v. Biggins, 507 U.S. 604 (1993)), but Kessler's phrasing undercuts it.
- Charge deadline 300 days (Illinois); EEOC/IDHR proceed despite arbitration (EEOC v. Waffle House, 534 U.S. 279 (2002)).

6. WORKERS' COMPENSATION RETALIATION - MODERATE-HIGH
- Claim 4/3/24 (shoulder; 15-lb restriction; no lost time). Termination within two months supports a Kelsay/4(h) claim with punitive damages; the plan's earlier origin helps causation, but the claim compounds exposure. The restriction also raises ADA/IHRA disability issues (unanalyzed). Comp benefits cannot be released without Commission approval (820 ILCS 305/23).

7. PRETEXT: PIP AND PERFORMANCE RECORD - HIGH
- Handbook 5.2.3 requires written closure and bars termination before closure; none exists. Kolb (34): extension, written failure notice, response opportunity, terminated seven months after NI with six months' severance. Okafor (41): extended, closed, retained. Washington (58): no extension, no closure, decision three days after expiry. Comparators are lower-level, so "similarly situated" is contestable (Coleman v. Donahoe, 667 F.3d 835 (7th Cir. 2012)), but departure from written policy is independent pretext evidence.
- Merits: Southern delays outside his control (Handbook 5.2.1 requires adjusting for that); cost target set unilaterally by the CI team and measured over 47 days; HR itself rated two objectives "meaningful progress." PIP cites Handbook "7.4" (PIP rules are 5.2). File lacks the 4/17 interim assessment and check-in summaries. No prior counseling before the NI review. Record: 19 reviews, five "Exceeds," two Leader-of-the-Year awards.
- Shifting rationales (performance, restructuring, Cause) are themselves pretext evidence; the restructuring plan was "ready" before the PIP concluded.

8. THE "RESTRUCTURING" RATIONALE IS WEAK
- Duties pass to Ostrowski (same 12 facilities, about 480 staff) and a new Director takes the six Regional Managers: a replacement, not an elimination.
- Financials: the memo claims +$132,550, but its table sums to $566,500 (356,500 + 210,000), not $520,000; the true increase over $387,450 is about $179,050. Cost savings cannot justify it, and the memo also blames Washington's missed target.
- Kessler says the Board "has reviewed" and is "supportive"; the memo only requests approval, and no minutes or vote are in the file.

9. CONTRACT (Employment Agreement 6/15/2016; Illinois law)
- Without Cause (s.4.2): 30 days' prior written notice delivered per s.8.5, so June 10 is unavailable; no pay-in-lieu clause. Severance, conditioned on Release: 12 months' base ($287,000), pro-rata target bonus (about $44,500 through 6/10: 162/366 x $100,450; "actual performance" ambiguity), 12 months' COBRA (about $28,080 at the 2016 $2,340 estimate; update), outplacement up to $15,000. Total about $375,000. Restructuring is without Cause. Non-renewal is also treated as without Cause (s.3.1), and the 90-day window for the June 15, 2024 renewal has passed.
- For Cause (s.4.3) is unsupported: no felony, willful misconduct causing material harm, or dishonesty; no breach notice with 30-day cure; (v) requires written notice and 30+ days' cure, and the unclosed PIP is the only candidate (partial success, factors beyond his control). Cause also requires a Board majority vote at a convened meeting, written statement 10 business days beforehand, and a hearing; none has occurred. Asserting Cause after the 6/3 email invites bad-faith/pretext findings, breach damages, and Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act exposure (820 ILCS 115).
- Good Reason (s.4.5): stripping duties or changing his reporting line triggers resignation with identical severance; no advantage in staging.
- Release (Ex. A): 21/7 days satisfies OWBPA for an individual (29 U.S.C. 626(f)(1)); a group program (two or more employees) requires 45 days and disclosures. It omits OSH Act, Whistleblower Act and comp claims, cannot bar agency charges, and an 11(c) resolution needs OSHA approval. New confidentiality terms must meet the Workplace Transparency Act (820 ILCS 96). He may refuse to sign and sue.
- Covenants (Art. 5): 18-month/150-mile non-compete and 24-month non-solicits apply even after a without-Cause termination. Pre-2022 agreement, so common law applies (Reliable Fire Equipment v. Arredondo, 2011 IL 111871); enforceability against a retaliatorily terminated employee is uncertain. Consider narrowing as a bargaining chip.
- Arbitration (s.7.1): AAA, Chicago, individual basis, covering statutory and tort claims; injunctive relief carve-out. It does not bar agency proceedings; it limits jury risk.

10. PRIVILEGE AND PRESERVATION
- HR notes, 5/20-5/22 emails, Kessler's 6/3 email and the Board memo are business records; copying Ms. Morales or labelling them privileged will likely not protect them. The OSHA file's "work product" label covers only counsel's compilation. Chandrasekaran is a credible adverse witness. Issue a litigation hold now; stop email commentary; route Cause strategy through counsel. Kessler is the key actor; the Board should receive advice directly.

11. DOCUMENT INCONSISTENCIES
- Entity: Agreement parties are Saxonbrook Logistics Solutions, Inc., but the signature block and other documents use Vanguard Logistics Solutions, Inc. ("VLS"); confirm the contracting entity (s.8.4). Signature lines are blank in the copies; obtain executed originals.
- Agreement names Brannigan as CEO; the review says he did the February 2023 review though Kessler became CEO 1/1/23. Handbook s.6.4 (rebuttal) and 7.4 (PIP) are not in the excerpts; get the full Handbook. Employee IDs differ across documents. Chandrasekaran is "SVP" in one email, "VP" elsewhere. Workers' comp form dates hands-on work as 2002-2007 and as through 2012. "19 reviews" over 22 years is unexplained. Salary still $287,000 since 2016; confirm.

12. LIMITS
Case and statute pinpoints are from knowledge; the eCFR was inaccessible and the Whistleblower Act amendment was checked only through secondary summaries. Verify before reliance. If action occurs after 1/1/2025, apply the amended Act.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Suspend the June 10 date; no termination pending counsel review.
2. Issue a litigation hold; instruct Kessler, Ostrowski and HR to stop commentary on Washington.
3. Commission an independent outside-counsel investigation of retaliation and age issues; confirm Kessler's knowledge date and Ostrowski's age.
4. Formally close or extend the PIP in writing (30 days, per HR), allow Southern rollout completion, and correct the cost objective.
5. Give the Board the complete record (HR 5/22 concerns, comparators, corrected financials, Safety Committee report) for a convened vote.
6. Do not assert Cause. Either terminate under s.4.2 on 30 days' notice or negotiate a mutual separation: severance at or above s.4.2, OSHA-approved settlement, tailored OWBPA-compliant release with agency and comp carve-outs, reduced covenants, agreed messaging. Compare about $375,000 plus premium against back/front pay, double liquidated and punitive damages, fees and OSHA scrutiny.
7. Correct the restructuring memo's arithmetic and language; preserve the original.
8. Implement Safety Committee recommendations on Changes 1 and 3 and updated hazard analyses (general-duty clause; 29 C.F.R. 1910.178).
9. Verify entity, executed documents and Handbook; assess disability issues from the shoulder restriction.
